items.prompt: A team wants a server-side layer that fans out to several backend services and reshapes the combined result for exactly one type of client. What's this pattern called?
choices: API gateway
Backend for Frontend (BFF)
Service mesh
Load balancer
items.explanation: A BFF is defined by exactly this: a thin layer, specific to one client type, that calls several backend services and combines/reshapes their responses into what that one client needs.
items.reference:
Mobile BFF

combines price+stock+reviews for one cellular round trip

Web BFF

combines the same data, shaped differently

Why: one BFF per client type is what lets each get exactly the shape it needs, without a shared endpoint negotiating between them.

items.prompt: Which best describes what a Backend for Frontend (BFF) does?
choices: A client-agnostic layer handling auth and routing for every client
Aggregates and reshapes backend responses for one specific frontend
A read-replica database used for scaling reads
A CDN edge cache for static assets
items.explanation: Aggregation and client-specific reshaping is the BFF's whole job. Auth/routing for every client is the API gateway's job, not the BFF's.
items.reference:
Mobile BFF

combines price+stock+reviews for one cellular round trip

Web BFF

combines the same data, shaped differently

Why: one BFF per client type is what lets each get exactly the shape it needs, without a shared endpoint negotiating between them.

items.prompt: Mobile needs a slim combined payload; web needs a differently-shaped payload from the same underlying data. What pattern lets each client get exactly what it needs, without the other one's requirements getting in the way?
choices: A single shared REST endpoint with optional query parameters
One BFF per client type
A bigger database
Removing the web client entirely
items.explanation: A shared endpoint with optional parameters still forces one team's shape changes to risk breaking the other client. A BFF per client type removes that coupling entirely — each BFF only has to satisfy its own client.
items.reference:
Mobile BFF

combines price+stock+reviews for one cellular round trip

Web BFF

combines the same data, shaped differently

Why: one BFF per client type is what lets each get exactly the shape it needs, without a shared endpoint negotiating between them.

items.prompt: Which of these is a job for an API gateway, not a BFF?
choices: Aggregating 3 services into 1 response
Rate limiting and authentication for every client
Reshaping a response for one mobile screen
Combining reviews and inventory data for a product page
items.explanation: Rate limiting and auth are cross-cutting, client-agnostic concerns — exactly the API gateway's job. Aggregating and reshaping for a specific screen is what the BFF does.
items.reference:

Client-awareNoYes

Why: a gateway serves every client the same way; a BFF exists precisely because different clients need different things.

items.prompt: Which statement is correct?
choices: The BFF is client-agnostic; the API gateway is client-specific
The API gateway is client-agnostic; the BFF is client-specific
Both are always the exact same service
Neither one ever handles authentication
items.explanation: It's the gateway that's the same for every client (auth, rate limiting, routing); the BFF is deliberately built per client type to reshape data for that client's screens.

The web BFF
The API gateway
reviews-service
items.explanation: Auth and TLS termination apply uniformly to every client, which is the definition of an API gateway's job — putting it in a specific BFF would mean duplicating it in every other BFF too.

items.prompt: Who typically owns and maintains a given BFF?
choices: The platform/infra team
The frontend team that consumes it
The database team
No one — it's auto-generated from the API schema
items.explanation: A BFF is scoped to one frontend's needs, so it's typically owned by (or closely aligned with) that frontend team — that's what removes the cross-team negotiation over a shared endpoint's shape.
items.reference:
Mobile BFF → owned near the mobile team. Web BFF → owned near the web team. Gateway → owned by platform/infra.

Why: ownership follows who actually needs to change the shape quickly — the frontend team shipping the screen.

items.prompt: A redesign of the mobile product screen needs a new field in its aggregated response. Whose code most directly needs to change?
choices: The API gateway team's
The mobile BFF's
reviews-service's, only
No code needs to change
items.explanation: The mobile BFF is where the screen-specific aggregation logic lives, so a new field for that screen is a change scoped to the mobile BFF — that's the whole point of splitting it out from a shared endpoint.
items.reference:
Mobile BFF → owned near the mobile team. Web BFF → owned near the web team. Gateway → owned by platform/infra.

Why: ownership follows who actually needs to change the shape quickly — the frontend team shipping the screen.

items.prompt: A shared REST API returns one resource per endpoint. A mobile screen that needs 4 resources, without a BFF, has to make how many sequential round trips before it can render?
items.explanation: Without an aggregation layer, each resource is its own round trip — 4 resources means 4 separate requests before the screen has everything it needs.
items.reference:
Without BFF

4 sequential calls, ~880ms

With BFF

1 call, ~220ms

Why: chattiness is literally counted in round trips — moving the fan-out server-side is what collapses 4 into 1.

items.prompt: What's the term for an API that forces a client to make many small round trips to assemble a single screen?
choices: A chatty API
A stateless API
An idempotent API
A RESTful API
items.explanation: "Chatty" describes exactly this: many small back-and-forth calls needed to get one meaningful result, as opposed to a coarser call that returns what's actually needed in one trip.
items.reference:
Without BFF

4 sequential calls, ~880ms

With BFF

1 call, ~220ms

Why: chattiness is literally counted in round trips — moving the fan-out server-side is what collapses 4 into 1.

items.prompt: Why does moving the fan-out server-side, into a BFF, typically reduce a screen's total load time compared to the client making the calls itself?
choices: Server-to-server calls are usually much lower latency than client-to-server calls over a cellular or public network
Server calls are free and client calls cost money
It removes the need for authentication entirely
It reduces the number of backend services that exist
items.explanation: The client's round trip crosses a slow, variable public network (or cellular). Once the fan-out happens inside the data center, service-to-service calls are typically much faster — the client then only pays one slow round trip instead of several.
items.reference:
Without BFF

With BFF

1 call, ~220ms

Why: chattiness is literally counted in round trips — moving the fan-out server-side is what collapses 4 into 1.

items.prompt: What problem does contract testing solve once a system is split into a BFF and several independently deployed domain services?
choices: It makes every service run faster
It lets services deploy independently while still catching breaking changes before they ship
It replaces the need for an API gateway
It removes the need for a BFF entirely
items.explanation: Splitting into independent services creates a new risk: one service's change silently breaking another. Contract testing catches that risk fast, without forcing services back into lockstep deploys.
items.reference:
Consumer (BFF) records what it needs → provider (domain service) checks its real responses against that, in its own CI, before every deploy.

Why: the whole point is catching breakage fast without forcing a slow, shared integration test.

items.prompt: A reviews-service team wants to know if a planned change would break the mobile BFF — without spinning up the mobile app or a shared staging environment. What tool fits this need?
choices: A full end-to-end test suite
A consumer-driven contract test
A load test
A manual QA pass on staging
items.explanation: That's exactly what a consumer-driven contract test is for: verify the provider's real handler against what the consumer recorded it needs, with neither service's full stack actually running.
items.reference:
Consumer (BFF) records what it needs → provider (domain service) checks its real responses against that, in its own CI, before every deploy.

Why: the whole point is catching breakage fast without forcing a slow, shared integration test.

items.prompt: Why can't an API gateway alone solve mobile's chattiness problem from the opening scenario?
choices: Gateways are too slow to be useful

items.prompt: In consumer-driven contract testing between the mobile BFF and reviews-service, who is the 'consumer'?
choices: reviews-service
The mobile BFF
The API gateway
The end user's phone
items.explanation: The consumer is whoever calls the other service and depends on its response shape — here, the mobile BFF calling reviews-service. The consumer writes the contract describing what it needs.

Why: "consumer-driven" means the consumer's real usage defines the contract, not the provider's full schema.

A manual QA engineer, by hand

items.prompt: reviews-service adds a brand-new topReviewIds field that the mobile BFF's contract never mentions. What happens to the mobile BFF's existing contract test?
choices: It fails, because the response schema changed
It still passes — the contract only covers fields the consumer actually reads
It can no longer run at all
It silently ignores every field, including the ones it used to check
items.explanation: A consumer-driven contract only asserts what the consumer actually depends on. A field the mobile BFF never reads can be added freely without breaking its contract — that's what lets providers extend their API safely.
items.reference:
Contract: "response has numeric averageRating and integer reviewCount." Nothing about topReviewIds — so adding it changes nothing for this contract.

Why: narrow contracts are what make them fast and non-brittle — they check only what would actually break the consumer.

items.prompt: Why does a consumer-driven contract test intentionally avoid checking the provider's entire response schema?
choices: Because writing a full schema check would be too slow to author
Because it only needs to guarantee what the consumer actually depends on, so providers stay free to extend their responses
Because JSON schemas can't be represented in a contract file
Because full schema checks aren't supported by any testing tool
items.explanation: Checking the full schema would fail every time the provider adds anything new, even fields no consumer reads — which would turn every provider deploy into a coordination problem again, the exact thing contract testing exists to avoid.
items.reference:
Contract: "response has numeric averageRating and integer reviewCount." Nothing about topReviewIds — so adding it changes nothing for this contract.

Why: narrow contracts are what make them fast and non-brittle — they check only what would actually break the consumer.

items.prompt: A fifth domain service (promotions-service) launches, and mobile's product screen now needs its data too. Which layer needs a code change?

reviews-service

items.prompt: Why does adding a new domain service call to one screen NOT require changing the API gateway?

Gateways are read-only infrastructure by design
Gateways don't allow new backend services to exist
items.explanation: The gateway routes traffic to the right BFF and enforces policy that's the same for everyone — it has no reason to know or care which domain services that BFF fans out to internally.
items.reference:
Adding promotions-service to the product page → new outbound call + new field, inside the mobile BFF only. Gateway, other services untouched.

Why: screen-specific change should cost a screen-specific edit, not touch shared infrastructure everyone depends on.

items.reference:

Why: screen-specific change should cost a screen-specific edit, not touch shared infrastructure everyone depends on.

items.explanation: Checking only requiredFields, and ignoring anything else on response, is exactly what makes a consumer-driven contract narrow: a provider adding new fields (like topReviewIds) never breaks a consumer that never asked for them, which is what lets providers extend their API freely.
items.reference:
Contract checks: does response have averageRating (number) and reviewCount (number)? It never asks whether response has ONLY those fields.

Why: checking a subset, not an exact match, is what keeps a contract from breaking on every unrelated provider change.
